overview: Two next-generation CRISPR-derived genome-editing technologies that avoid double-strand breaks, differing in scope and flexibility of the edits they can make.
genZNote: Base editing swaps one letter. Prime editing rewrites whole words without breaking the page.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: Uses a catalytically impaired Cas9 fused to a deaminase enzyme to directly convert one DNA base to another without cutting both strands.
aspects.valueB: Uses a Cas9 nickase fused to a reverse transcriptase and a prime editing guide RNA (pegRNA) to directly write new genetic information into a target site.

aspects.label: Scope of Possible Edits
aspects.valueA: Limited to specific base conversions — cytosine base editors (C-to-T) and adenine base editors (A-to-G).
aspects.valueB: Highly versatile — can perform all 12 possible base-to-base conversions, plus small insertions and deletions.

aspects.label: Double-Strand Breaks
aspects.valueA: Avoids double-strand breaks entirely, minimizing large indels.
aspects.valueB: Also avoids double-strand breaks, using a nick-and-write mechanism instead.

aspects.label: Precision / Editing Window
aspects.valueA: Edits within a defined window near the target site; can produce unwanted "bystander" edits of nearby bases.
aspects.valueB: Highly precise, defined edits with minimal bystander effects, though efficiency can be lower.

aspects.label: Applications
aspects.valueA: Correcting point mutations caused by a single specific base change (e.g. some forms of sickle cell disease research).
aspects.valueB: Correcting a broader range of mutations, including insertions, deletions, and all substitution types, for research and therapeutic development.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: Converts one specific base to another directly.
aspects.valueB: Writes new, flexible genetic sequences using a reverse transcriptase and pegRNA.
